subtopic: REPORT ON SECOND PART OP FIRST SESSION OF GENERAL ASSEMBLY

speechtext:
Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Secretary of State for External Affairs): Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to table the report on the second part of the first session of the general assembly of the united nations which was held in New York from October 23 to December 15 last year. Copies of the report are being circulated to all members of the house. The present copies of the report are in English; a French edition is in preparation.
Though the report is formally a report on the New \rork meeting of the assembly, it is in fact more than that. The discussions of some issues in New York were part of a process of study and discussion which had gone

United Nations
on in various bodies of the united nations since the end of the first part of the first session of the assembly in London. The report therefore covers many of the developments in the united nations during the whole period from the close of the London meeting on February 14, 1946 until the close of the New York meeting on December 15, 1946. This is indicated in the title of the report, which is "The United Nations, 1946".
The report is the third in the series of reports which the Department of External Affairs has issued on the united nations. The first report was on the San Francisco conference and the second report on the London meeting of the assembly. Together, those three reports describe the progress of the united nations and Canada's participation in it from the opening of the San Francisco conference to the end of 1946.
In many ways, this report is a departure from ordinary practice. It is not merely that it is more extensive but it is more explanatory and more outspoken.
Frankness is, I think, appropriate in a report of the united nations from the government of Canada to the parliament and people of Canada. The charter of the united nations begins with the words "We, the peoples of the United Nations". The charter thus recognizes a very direct relation between the united nations and the individual citizen of the member states. It is, therefore, fitting that the Canadian government should give to the citizens of Canada a full account of its steward' ship in respect of the united nations.
The report contains not only a summary of the discussions and decisions of the assembly but also the text of the more important resolutions adopted by the assembly. It tells how Canada voted on about forty of the more important or the more controversial issues and gives the reasons why the Canadian representatives voted as they did. It also gives the text of the more important speeches made by Canadian representatives at the plenary meetings of the assembly and in the committees.
The report is a lengthy document and perhaps the members of the house w'ould allow me to draw attention to some of the sections which might be of particular interest.
The preface to the report explains the structure of the united nations and of the various bodies linked to it. We thought that this might be useful because the structure is somewhat complex.
This is followed by a general survey of the work which the assembly was able to accom-83166-119j
plish in New York. Perhaps I might mention some of the conclusions set forth in that survey.
More was accomplished in New York than could reasonably have been expected when the assembly opened. The assembly demonstrated that, when it had delicate political questions to deal with, it would usually deal with them with moderation and restraint. Usually, not always. It would be too much to expect of any deliberative body, when it is dealing with questions which arouse deep feelings, that it should always act with moderation and restraint. Appeals to passion and prejudice were made, for example, in the debates on the Spanish question and on the treatment of Indians in South Africa. These appeals were not confined to the advocates of any particular resolution.
Under present conditions issues like the Spanish and South African issues cannot be properly settled in a deliberative body such as the assembly by counting heads. Unfortunately this truth was not always recognized in the discussion of these issues but it was recognized in the discussions on disarmament. What appears to be the most important accomplishment of the assembly in New York was the unanimous adoption of the resolution on disarmament, and this unanimity was made possible only by the joint and sustained efforts of many delegations to reconcile the separate proposals which each had advanced. These efforts were based on a common recognition of the fact that, if an assembly resolution on disarmament was to have practical results, it had to be concurred in by all the heavily armed powers and by the great majority of all the other powers.
One encouraging feature of the assembly was that in voting on important questions there were few hard and fast blocs of states. To demonstrate this, we have included in the report an appendix showing how each of the 54 members of the united nations voted on ten significant issues. This table is worthy, I think, of careful study.
The general survey of the work of the assembly is supplemented by a somewhat similar survey of the work of the economic and social council. The structure of organized intergovernmental cooperation on economic and social questions is more complex today than before the war. In addition to the economic and social organs of the united nations itself there are at present seven, and there may soon be twelve, international organizations which are specialized and functional and to which large areas of international collaboration have been entrusted. It is hoped that this great
United Nations

series of organizations will provide for comprehensive and varied attack on those economic and social problems to the solution of which international collaboration can contribute. The range and complexity of the system, however, carry with them certain dangers. The report sets forth some of these dangers as we see them and some of the ways in which they might be minimized.
One of the dangers is that, because of the increasing number of international meetings and their increasing length, governments may find it difficult to send adequate delegations to all the meetings. It was for this reason that the Canadian government had included in the agenda of the assembly in New York an item entitled "measures to economize the time of the general assembly". Our views on this question, to which we attach considerable importance, are set forth fully in the report.
The general survey is followed by sections dealing with each of the main issues which arose in New York. These are grouped under six heads-political, economic and social, trusteeship, administrative and budgetary, legal, and other questions.
I shall not attempt to list these questions. I would, however, like to draw the special attention of the members of the house to the section on disarmament.
We feel that Canada was able to make a valuable contribution to the discussions in New York. On this question and in order that the record may speak for itself, we have included in the appendix to the report the text of the final disarmament resolution together with the various preceding drafts including the Canadian proposals. We have also included the speeches given by Canadian representatives in explanation of the Canadian proposals. It seems clear that, had the assembly adopted a disarmament resolution wrhich contained the imperfections and ambiguities present in the original proposals, the debates, which would have been precipitated in the security council and the atomic energy commission on the precise meaning of the words of the resolution and exactly what the assembly had recommended the security council and the atomic energy commission to do, would have been long, harassing, and probably sterile.
As members of the house who have attended international conferences know, a great deal of the most useful work of a delegation does not appear on the surface of events. Perhaps the proportion that rises above the surface is very much the same as the proportion of an iceberg which is above the surface of the water.
As an indication of this, we have thought it wise to include in the report the text of the

"working paper" on disarmament which was prepared in the Canadian delegation over three weeks before we formally submitted to the assembly our resolution on disarmament. We have also printed for the first time the memorandum on sanctions and the veto which the Canadian delegation to the atomic energy commission circulated to the commission on December 19.
Questions have been raised about Canada's attitude on the various issues which have arisen in the united nations concerning relations with the present regime in Spain. I think that hon. members will find that these questions are fully dealt with in the report. There is, for example, a statement of the position which Canada took on each of fourteen votes on the Spanish question.
In the hope that it might be of assistance to the special committee of both houses which is to be set up to study the question of human rights and fundamental freedoms, we have included in the report the statement of essential human rights which was drawn up [DOT]by a committee appointed by the American Law Institute, the resolution of the assembly referring that statement to the commission on human rights, and the resolution of the economic and social council establishing the human rights commission.
During this session of parliament, the house may be asked to consider various questions relating to refugees and international relief. There are sections in the report dealing with these questions which might provide useful background material for the members.
The same applies to the sections in the report on the budget of the united nations and on the scale of contributions to those budgets.
The Canadian delegation to the assembly in New York .contained members not only from the government side but also from the Progressive Conservative and C.C.F. parties. I should like to take advantage of this opportunity to express on behalf of the government our appreciation of the contribution which was made to the work of the delegation in New York by the leader of the opposition in this house and the leader of the opposition in the Senate and by the leader in this house of the C.C.F. party. We worked together as a team in New York. We discussed fully and frankly at daily meetings the problems with which the delegation was confronted.
This policy of sending to the general assembly of the united nations a delegation representing all the major political parties of Canada is an experiment. Under our system of government, the government of the day must accept full responsibility for every action of a delegation at an international conference.

United Nations
That responsibility must be ours and we do not ask the opposition parties to share it. We do feel, however, that it is of immense value to the people of Canada .to have leading members of the opposition parties participate at the united nations assembly in the discussions which lead up to decisions on the attitude which the Canadian delegation should take.
Pending the time when we may be able to have a discussion in this house of Canada's relations with the united nations, it might be appropriate to have this report considered by the standing committee on external affairs and, if I have the unanimous consent of the house, I should be glad to move that the report now tabled be referred to that committee.	.

maintopic: SEASONAL DELIVERY QUOTAS ON BASIS OF SEEDED ACREAGE

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. MacKINNON (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: SEASONAL DELIVERY QUOTAS ON BASIS OF SEEDED ACREAGE
speechtext:
I wish to make a brief statement in regard to the basis of wheat deliveries in western Canada. Members of the house will recall that since August 1, 1941 wheat delivery quotas have been based upon what was known as the authorized acreage. An authorized acreage was established covering each farm unit in western Canada and delivery quotas were established on the basis of so many bushels per authorized acre. Authorized acreages were more equitable than seeded acreages whenever there was a possibility of a final limitation on producers' wheat deliveries in any crop year. Because it is not the intention of the government finally to limit wheat deliveries, it has been thought advisable on grounds of equity to use a seeded acreage basis in 1947-48.
Under the conditions which now exist the government is of the view that for the crop year 1947-48 and until further notice, any seasonal delivery quotas necessary for wheat and other grains in western Canada will be based on seeded acreage.
I am making this statement at this time in order that grain producers in the west may understand that any seasonal delivery quotas which may be established in the coming crop year will be on a seeded acreage basis for wheat and other grains.

subtopic: DISBANDMENT-EXPRESSIONS OF THANKS ON BEHALF OF CANADIAN PEOPLE

speakeroldname: Hon. BROOKE CLANTON (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: DISBANDMENT-EXPRESSIONS OF THANKS ON BEHALF OF CANADIAN PEOPLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if the house will permit I should like to make a statement with respect to the veterans guard.
	.
Another stage has been reached in the demobilization of Canada's armed forces. We have already said good-bye to such fine wartime organizations as the Women's Royal Canadian Naval Service, the Canadian Women's Army Corps and the Women's Division of the Royal Canadian Air Force, better known with affectionate respect as the WREN's, the CWAC's and the W.D.'s. Now it is with feelings of pride that I call the attention of this house to the work of that splendid body of men, the veterans guard of Canada, due for disbandment today.
The veterans guard was authorized during the dark days of May 1940 to give the veterans of the war of 1914-1918 their chance to serve in the defence of the home front. They stood on guard for Canada in the front line trenches of 1914-1918 and in the second world war they stood on guard for Canada on the frontiers of their native land.
Amongst the tasks which their country asked them to undertake during the recent war was the protection of many lonely but important places on both the Atlantic and Pacific coasts and many vital and vulnerable points in Canada where sabotage or any form of enemy attack might have been a national calamity. These men, too, willingly undertook one of the most wearing, tiring and thankless of all tasks with the firm discipline which they themselves had learned as Canadian soldiers, and, with the tact and humanity which they had learned as Canadian citizens, they guarded the enemy prisoners of war and escorted them back to Europe when the war was over.
In October 1941 the first members of the corps proceeded overseas for duty at Canadian military headquarters, in London, and other companies soon followed. A special detachment was sent to Newfoundland early in 1942 and companies were sent to the West Indies and British Guiana.
In the ranks of the veterans guard were men who had gallantly led their comrades into successful action in the great war of 1914-1918. Their ranks were decorated with the ribbons of two Victoria Crosses, 65 Military Crosses and bars, more than 75 Distinguished Conduct Medals and over 300 Military Medals.
At the peak strength in August 1945, nearly
9,000	veterans were serving in the veterans guard. Some of these men spent ten of the last thirty years serving their country in two world wars. Those thirty years should under happier circumstances have been the happiest and most productive of their lives, dedicated to peaceful tasks and the joys of family union. The fact that ten out of thirty years should have been spent in this way is a challenge

Veterans Guard of Canada
not only to us but to the whole world of men to work with each other and with all nations, in order that such devotion and unselfish service can hereafter be dedicated, not to the harassing duties of war but to the advancement of national, international and human welfare.
On behalf of the Canadian people, I extend to the Veterans Guard of Canada heartfelt thanks for a good job well done, and a grateful farewell.
With regard to the demobilization of the remaining men in the three services who enlisted for the duration of the war or for interim service, a relatively small number are being retained, with their consent, until the end of September of this year to assist in putting the armed forces on a post-war basis. As this phase is completed, the men so serving will be progressively reduced and all will be out of uniform by September 30, 1947. This is the date by which every man who joined up for the duration of the war will have returned to civilian employment or enlisted in the post-war active forces.
This termination date will be marked by appropriate ceremonies, particularly to recognize the part played by Canada's reserve forces in our total war effort and to emphasize the great part that the naval reserve divisions, the Canadian army reserve force and the air force auxiliary squadrons can, and we trust, will, play in the post-war forces which should the need arise again will be available to serve our country. Every fit young man too young to serve in war should join one of Canada's citizen services. The reserve forces are proceeding with their organization and their essential place in Canada's national life in peace and war calls for strong support in every community.

speechtext:
Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Secretary of State for External Affairs)-: I would ask for the consent of the house to move at this time the motion of which notice is printed on page 27 of the routine proceedings and orders of the day. W'hen the house took recess some time after six -o'clock on Friday, the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon), who was then acting for the leader of the opposition, asked the leader of the house to indicate the programme of work for today; that was done, and it seemed to me to meet with pretty general satisfaction as being a proper programme for this day. But it so happens that that programme cannot be carried out in accordance with the standing orders of the house unless this motion printed on page 27 of the routine proceedings and orders of the day is considered at this time. There had been a motion made that government notices of motion have precedence over all other matters, but the introduction of bills, questions, notices of motions for the production of papers. But the effect of that resolution expired on Friday the 28th, and we would therefore, under normal procedure, revert to the standing orders which would be in accord with the proceedings as printed in the orders of the day.
I discussed this with several members of the house and it was suggested, amongst other things, that in making this motion at this time, the exception providing for the introduction of bills, questions and notices of motions for the production of papers should be extended and should include, from eight to nine o'clock in the evening on Tuesday and Fridays, private bills and public bills. That seemed to be a reasonable suggestion, and if I have the consent of the house to make the

Business of the House
motion at this time I should be disposed to include that exception in the motion, so that on Tuesdays and Fridays from eight to nine o'clock private bills and members' public bills might be considered-in accordance with standing orders so long as government business has precedence over other matters.
There is another feature which was pointed out to me, which I in turn discussed with my colleagues, and which we found was quite proper. I do not think any member of the house considers it to be entirely fair that private members should be deprived of the opportunity of bringing before the house matters which might not be on the routine proceedings and orders of the day. Having discussed that with my colleagues I am prepared to give the undertaking that so long as government business would have precedence under a resolution such as this, the government would as the first order of government business on each Monday move the house into committee of supply so that all hon. members would have at that time a full opportunity to air any grievances which they might have or to bring to the attention of the house anything not on the routine proceedings and orders of the day which they felt was of sufficient importance to engage the attention of the house at that time. I think it would be well if each Monday that is to be taken for government business, as the first order of government business there were a motion to go into committee of supply, so that every hon. member would have an opportunity to bring up at that time anything which he felt was of sufficient importance to warrant its being discussed. The intention of the government would not be to go on with the consideration of supply when the house got into committee, but rather to call two or three departments and have them opened so that they might on any appropriate occasion be dealt with in accordance with the standing orders.
If that arrangement seemed to be suitable, it might be taken as an undertaking of the government to move, on every Monday when government business would have precedence over other affairs, to go into committee of supply as the first order of business so that any question not on the order paper but about which any hon. member was concerned, could be discussed. We have now only today, tomorrow and a short day on Wednesday before taking recess and I think it was the general feeling that we should continue with the emergency legislation before the house. I would therefore request leave to move at this time:
That on Monday, March 31 instant and every sitting day thereafter until and including Monday, April 28 next, government notices of motions and government orders shall have precedence over all other business except introduction of bills, questions and notices of motions for the production of papers, and except, from eight to nine o'clock in the evening on Tuesdays and Fridays, private and public bills; and that standing order No. 15 be suspended in relation thereto.

The acting leader of the government has indicated the position in which we find ourselves today as a result of the way in which our programme is printed in the routine proceedings. The procedure allows private members' business to have priority over government business. The minister has suggested that we reverse that order and put government business before private members' business. As he has indicated and as we all know, in order that the change may be made now, notice not having been given before, the arrangement must have the unanimous approval of the house.
Speaking for the official opposition, when requests of this kind have been made to us, as has been the case several times this session, we have raised no objection, and we raise no objection now. I think it only fair, however, to point out what the minister himself indicated, namely, that particularly during this session private members have been asked to make sacrifices, and there should be some recognition of the position in which they have been placed. We have no desire to take advantage of the technical position in which the government finds itself today. I do not think we should. And I do not mean to urge the government to grant any more concessions to private members than their judgment would suggest. But the minister has said that from now on the government is willing to move to go into supply each Monday. To that extent private members will be permitted to discuss questions they feel should be dealt with. I think that is a good suggestion, and I support it. It is an ill wind that blows no one good, so if the situation confronting us today is a little difficult, I believe some good may come out of it for the private members of this house.
We are agreeable to the. suggestion reversing the order of business today, provided that free discussion is permitted each Monday when the motion is made to go into supply, and provided that we are not denied the right to discuss matters mentioned in private members' resolutions, which under a narrow technical interpretation of the rules I understand might be denied us. subtopic: ORGANIZATIONS ADVOCATING OVERTHROW OF CONSTITUTED AUTHORITY
speechtext:
Explain.
Mr. LaCROIX: The communist party of Canada and the Labour-Progressive party of Canada and organizations with similar objectives and advocating the use of similar means of overthrowing constituted authority as developed in Canada under our constitution are a menace to the safety of the state and should be outlawed by an adequate provision of the criminal code. I wish to say a word or two on this section. I realize that in the main the compensation boards of the provinces, particularly Ontario, with which I am best acquainted, do give first-class satisfaction. If a man's leg or arm is cut off or his eye is out or he is otherwise disabled and that disablement is quite easily seen, he is taken care of without any difficulty. But many men are injured and have industrial diseases which are difficult to observe. I do not wish to say anything that would in any way reflect on the medical boards of the compensation boards, but I am not satisfied with all that they do. For instance I know of the case of a man who had worked in a foundry for eighteen years. Knowing, or at least I used to know, all about foundry practice-and I have not forgotten all of it-I am convinced that he could not work steadily in a foundry for eighteen years unless he were fit. This particular man had the misfortune to bump his knee into some obstruction, a truck, or a wheelbarrow or some other such obstruction which is all too frequently in the way of people working in factories.
As I said, he had been working in the foundry for eighteen years. Because of that accident he was knocked out. He received compensation for some length of time; I have forgotten how long, but that is neither here nor there. The compensation board had their medical men examine him, and they declared that the reason he could not work was that his heart was affected and that he had an arthritic condition which caused his leg and knee to swell, thereby making it impossible for him to work. He is in bad shape. I believe he is on the road to his grave. In my judgment his condition is an industrial disease. How can it be proved that it is not? He was healthy for eighteen years; made his living for that length of time and all of a sudden he bumps into a truck or some other obstruction. On being examined some time after- I do not know how long after-the medical board stated that he had an arthritic condition as well as a heart condition. If he has, who is to prove that it is not the result of his accident? He could not possibly work steadily for eighteen years in the foundry business unless he had been 100 per cent healthy.
A moulder uses his knees all the time. He must be strong and healthy or he could, not stand the smoke, soot and dust of a foundry. The particular man to whom I have referred has been discharged by the board. In my opinion he is suffering, from an industrial disease. When the medical board states that a man who is now unfit to work because of an
[Mr. Chevrier.l
injury received while at work has no more claim for compensation, I do not agree with them. I believe, as I tried to say the other night, that workmen who now have no appeal, should be given that right.
I believe there is provision for appeal in New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island. Elsewhere there is no appeal from the medical decision of the board. The medical staff of the compensation board are not, in my opinion, to be put in the same class as the family doctor, who does his utmost for his patients, and is sympathetic at all times, whereas a member of a medical board under the compensation law is a government employee and does not need to care a fig whether he satisfies the workmen or not. As a result, I am sorry to say, in my opinion, too often the workman does not receive what he is entitled to. I have known quite a number of men who afterwards died from the injury or disease they contracted while working in a factory. All I wish to say is that if the act does not allow any appeal-I believe it does in certain provinces-

I think the act should apply to such people so that the workmen will have the benefit of appeal in all the provinces and not only in three. If it is right in three provinces it is right in all. I am concerned about this because I have seen such regrettable things. I do not find fault with the board. In the great majority of cases they give satisfaction. They do excellent work and, after men recover from accidents, try to provide jobs for them. There is much that I could say complimentary to the compensation boards. As I said before, years ago I was one of those who strongly advocated the system because my association with large numbers of working men was such as to suggest to me the necessity for something of the kind, and I was happy later on to see provincial governments passing compensation laws. In the operation of the law, however, I have not been 100 per cent satisfied. Am I asking too much when I suggest that the same treatment should be meted out to all working men throughout Canada as is given those in the three provinces mentioned?

I was going to say
to my hon. friend that if there is appeal in the three provinces I mentioned-Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick and Yukon and northwest territories-it is because of provincial law. The point which he makes is the same one he raised the other evening when we were discussing this question. The Government Employees Compensation Act has proceeded on the basis of utilizing the services of provincial boards, and my hon. friend raised a point the other day when he said, "I hope the minister will not set up a whole new department". That is exactly what we do not want to do, but if we are to have an appeal court, then we must set up a whole new department.
As I understand compensation, it is a matter of property and civil rights to be dealt with by the provinces under the British North America Act. Not so, however, as regards government employees, and we in the Department of Transport have always proceeded on the basis that, while we had jurisdiction under the British North America Act, we should not undertake to set up a separate and different administration but rather should use the experience of the provincial boards which have existed. We have done that in Ontario and Quebec and in all the other provinces and have got along fairly satisfactorily.
In Ontario there is no appeal from the decision of the compensation board, and I presume the same position obtains in the province of Quebec. If we were to set up our own machinery in Ottawa, and proceeded to deal with these cases in the manner in which the boards deal with them across the provinces, then we would be doing exactly what my hon. friend the other evening did not want us to do when he expressed the fear that this would mean the establishment of a whole new department. I fear I have to tell him that, so long as we use the media which are at our disposal in the form of the provincial boards, we shall have to deal with the law as it exists in those provinces.
In the three provinces where there is an appeal court the decision of the officer or the board is subject to appeal, and in the other ' provinces, where there is no appeal court, unfortunately there is nothing under this act that we can do apart from what I have said, namely, setting up separate machinery, which would be costly.

Another point I would mention is the question of wage. It applies to an employee who is paid a direct wage or salary. I am going to ask the minister to explain later whether that direct wage will cover an hourly wage to a temporary or casual employee.
In order to bring this individual case to the attention of the minister in the hope that it will receive more consideration and more direct attention I must go back over correspondence which began in June, 1945. I will give the details as briefly as possible. The case received the. support and attention of the Canadian Legion, Halifax branch, and many letters have been written by individuals in connection with it. I have had it before the Department of National Defence for Naval Services, as well as the Department of Transport on more than one occasion. I refer to the case of Murray Leonard Bowser, naval civilian employee, who was first employed in Halifax as time and material recorder. He entered the employ of the government on November 9, 1942. After serving in Halifax, he was transferred to Quebec in February, 1943, and I wish the minister to make a note of that. He remained there until he was brought home sick in January, 1944.

subtopic: COMPENSATION FOR DISEASE, DISABILITY OR DEATH ARISING OUT OF EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
No, he was not a member of the Royal Canadian Navy. I will enlarge on that. He received his call-up on February, 1942, if I remember rightly and, finding that he was in category "E", he felt he would like like to enter some type of war work. He applied to H.M.C. dockyard, Halifax, where he was taken on as a civilian employee, as I stated, and engaged as time and material recorder. During the time he served in Quebec, while working on shipbuilding materials, he broke out with some type of skin disease; and several doctors claimed that the basic cause came from the work in which he was engaged.
Bowser has been confined to either hospital or his home since January, 1944, and during that time has been in a pretty serious condition. He is covered with sores from his feet to his head. He is unable to lie in bed without suffering great pain. His mother, who is a widow, has exhausted all her means and impaired her own health in caring for her son.

I hesitate to go into such details, but I know the minister will bear with me; I feel the case is so important, of such a serious and distressing type that I must go into details to a certain extent.
When Bowser was first employed he was to serve for the duration of the war and in any part of the world where his services might be required. While in Quebec he was admitted to hospital, but a few days later released, the doctors advising him that his disease would clear up in a few days. Remember, that was in 1942 and he is still suffering. Since then his condition has grown steadily worse. Today I am informed he has become totally blind and requires to be bandaged from feet to head.
As I stated, I have had his case repeatedly before the Department of National Defence; there was correspondence from September 7, 1945; a reply was received on October 9 of the same year. The Canadian Legion had the case before the deputy minister for naval services since June 22, 1945. The department is not willing to accept responsibility, and that is why I am pleased that this bill was introduced, because I thought this was likely a bill covering this special case, one that did not seem to come within the scope of the province of Quebec workmen's compensation act. By the way, the workmen's compensation commission of the province of Quebec would not accept any responsibility in this case, and that is why Bowser paid his own expenses, or rather his family were obliged to pay his expenses and transportation charges back to Halifax so that he could receive proper treatment there. What I want to know, if the minister will be good enough to tell me, is this. Will this bill cover a case of this type; and what will be the procedure to be followed to bring about the results desired, namely, a recognition of the liability of the government to deal with a case of this kind?
Bowser's illness, as stated, started in Quebec while he was on duty. He was transferred home at his own expense. His doctor bills, board and hospital charges have cost his aunt and mother something like $3,000. His mother is a widow, is not in good health and can ill afford to meet this heavy burden. The Quebec workmen's compensation commission rule that this disease is a form of eczema,' and eczema is not covered under the workmen's compensation act. I am questioning the minister whether it is covered in the term or interpretation mentioned in section 2 (b).
My late colleague, Mr. W. C. Macdonald, had the case reopened in October just prior to his passing to the great beyond, but a settlement had not been made up to the time

The object of the bill, as set out in the explanatory note, is to bring the act up to date. I should like to say a word with respect to the definitions. In the first place, this bill does not revise very much, as it should, the Government Employees' Compensation Act, which is chapter 30 of the revised statutes of Canada, 1927, as amended. There, has been a great war since that time, and these definitions are not nearly broad enough. Under this measure a man has to go to the workmen's compensation board, and follow through the whole procedure. Many of these men are among the lower paid government employees. If a man has a serious accident he may find that he is not covered by the. workmen's compensation board act of Ontario; if he dies his family may be put out on the street. Many of these men have given long service. Some were with the old Grand Trunk which was taken over by the Canadian National. During the last war many of these employees were working night and day on trains going to and from Halifax. Some contracted diseases; many were overworked. They were not paid any war bonus. So I should like to see this statute broadened to include Canadian National railway employees of this class, -who should be given some recognition for the fact that they often worked in demobilization eighteen hours a day. Many -were injured; many contracted diseases, throat trouble, lung trouble, and so on, which could be definitely traced to their long hours of toil by night and. by day, in all kinds of weather, both during the war and during demobilization. I do hope the government will consider these railway men, because they should be given some consideration.
In regard to the other features of the legislation, I believe the time has come when some appeal should be provided. As hon. members know, the workmen's compensation legislation is administered by a board, whose proceedings are very largely in private, with no one appearing for the applicant.

There is no definition in the bill of the words "injury by accident". As I read the bill, "injury by accident" by this section would mean only industrial disease. The bill does not provide that infectious disease is necessarily injury by accident. It is provided under the British workmen's compensation act-and this was decided by the courts over forty years ago- that an infectious disease not classified as an industrial disease may be an injury by accident. This bill contains no such provision, and it seems to me that the words "injury by accident" should be interpreted in the interpretation section in order that the boards which will administer these matters-there is no appeal from most of these boards-will have something to go by when it comes to interpreting those words.
We had some discussion about this matter last year when the bill to compensate merchant seamen was before the house. I do not want to go through all that again and I have not looked up the English cases since, but it does seem to me that there should be an interpretation of the words "injury by accident" which would be wide enough to include infectious diseases which are not classified as industrial diseases. It has been held in English cases for over forty years that the words "infectious diseases" come within the meaning of the act. I think we are not doing justice to the employees and workmen whom this bill is intended to protect unless we have a definition of that kind and unless we go so far as to provide in the act that infectious diseases in some cases at least are industrial diseases.

I have known many men in my time, as I am sure the hon. member for Huron-Perth has too, -with his wide experience in foundry machine-shop practice, who contracted tuberculosis perhaps through working in a damp part of the plant. The dampness and dust sometimes bring on tuberculosis, but it is impossible to get the boards to agree that the tuberculosis which these men contract is a result of their employment. I have known a number of them myself who contracted tuberculosis, as the family physician would certify. I have the highest regard for the family physician. His heart is with his patients. I agree to a large extent with what the hon. member for Temiscouata said in words much better than I could use in reference to medical boards set up by governments and doctors w-orking on government staffs. I want to be sure that section 8 covers those workmen who contract tuberculosis in a government institution outside a hospital, because they can contract tuberculosis working in a plant, and I can assure the minister that it is next to impossible to prove before any compensation board that the tuberculosis was contracted during the course of their employment. I should like to feel that this bill would cover the government's own workmen working in its own institutions other than hospitals. Take, for instance, the work the government is constructing on Snare river north of Yellowknife. Men there may fall into the water and contract tuberculosis through exposure. Those men should be protected by compensation just as much as the employees who contract tuberculosis through working in a sanatorium. I am interested in this matter because of a long association -with working men. I commend the government for what it is doing for the working man in this bill. The bill is wide and even goes outside Canada to protect government employees, and the minister deserves credit for that, but I should like to see it wide enough to cover the case of a workman, no matter where he may be, who contracts tuberculosis while working in any government plant, and if he dies his estate should have the right to compensation.

The other evening the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie) in his capacity as house leader, referred to the bill as a very short and easy bill. The hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) a little earlier this session made some passing reference to it. My attention was drawn to it a year ago when the bill passed through the house so quickly, in just a minute, that I did not have a chance to ask a question which was in the back of my mind. The question was, why should the government, by a government act or order, appoint a private auditor to audit the Canadian National Railways? Why does the auditor general not do this? During the past year I have had an opportunity of studying this matter at some length, and the completion of some study convinces me at least that the auditor general should do this job. I do not suggest that the firm of George A. Touche and Company do not do a good job. They do probably as good a job as any ordinary firm of auditors could do. But I am informed by auditors that there are two firms in Canada with a world-wide reputation which undoubtedly could do a better job. On the other hand, many firms undoubtedly could not do as good a job. I intend a little later to read a glowing testimonial to George A.
Touche and Company made by Doctor Man-ion when he was minister of railways. My point is not that the firm of George A. Touche and Company are not capable. My point is, first, that the auditor general should do the job; second, that he can do the job, and third, that he can do a much better job than any civilian auditor appointed by the government.
As far as the first point is concerned that he should do the job, I should like to touch briefly on the whole position of the auditor general. Here in parliament we have three principal servants of our own, men who are our servants and not the servants of the government-the Clerk of the House, the auditor general and the chief electoral officer. The former two are appointed, not by the governor in council, but by the governor of Canada under the great seal, and they can be removed, not by order in council, but only by an address of both houses of parliament. Beauchesne, the book not the Clerk, says that these two servants outrank any deputy minister in the government service. Of these two servants I think undoubtedly the auditor general is the more important. After all, taxation without representation has been the cause of most of the dissatisfaction, discontent and rebellion in our history, and certainly the control over public money is an important part of our system of government. It is to account to parliament that we have this watchdog of our own who is responsible only to us. It has not always been that way. Certainly the development of the position of the auditor general has gone step by step with the development of responsible government in Canada. In the days of the family compact there existed neither appropriations by the elected representatives nor the accounting to them of those appropriations. Back in 1835 the house set up the famous committee on grievances and William Lyon Mackenzie, in presenting its report in 1S35, made one or two remarks that I should like to repeat. He said:
I would impress upon the house the importance of two things:	first the necessity of getting control of the revenue raised in this country, and second a control over the men set out here to govern us by placing them under the direction of responsible advisers.
You will note that even in those days William Lyon Mackenzie put control of public money first.
At page 19 of the report of these grievances, a copy of which is kept under lock and key in the library, there is an elaboration of what was meant by control over revenue-not only a control over the passage of appropriations out of the public revenue, but a satisfactory audit of those expenditures.

C.N.R.-Appointment oj Auditors
The report would not recognize an audit by the government, or by auditors appointed by the government whose reports were described as "complex, obscure and unsatisfactory". An independent audit board was asked. It was not given, however, until 1855. Between 1835 and 1855 we had the rebellion, and then the Durham report and the beginnings of responsible government. But in the old Canada it was the minister of finance, known as the inspector general then, who actually did the auditing and told parliament everything was all right. However, in 1855 after a long debate the government of the day agreed to set up an independent audit board composed of the deputy ministers. This went along until 1878 when Alexander Mackenzie was premier, when the auditor general as we know him today was first set up independent of the political parties of the day and responsible only to parliament. The first auditor general was also comptroller general. Not only did he audit the final accounts for parliament, but before any appropriation could be spent he certified that the method of spending was in accord with parliament's will. This act of 1878 made the auditor general, in effect, an officer of parliament for the more complete examination of public accounts of the dominion and the reporting thereon to the House of Commons.
By 1931 it was agreed that it was not satisfactory to have our auditor general also comptroller, because he was checking up on his own work in that he had authorized the appropriation he was later auditing. Therefore the Consolidated Revenue Act was revised and the two duties separated, the comptroller general now being an officer of the Department of Finance and the auditor general being responsible solely to parliament and responsible for the audit of public accounts. This naturally resulted in a great improvement. The duties of the auditor general are listed in part V of the Consolidated Revenue Act of 1931. He is appointed by the governor general under the great seal and can be removed only by a joint address of both houses. His duties are listed in section 50 and are as follows:
In reporting the result of his examination and audit to the House of Commons, the auditor general shall call attention to every case in which
(a)	a grant has been exceeded;
(b)	moneys received from sources other than the grants for the year to which the account relates have not been applied or accounted for according to the direction of parliament; or
(c)	a sum charged against a grant is not supported by proof of payment.

And so on. And finally, "or to any other case which the auditor general considers should be brought to the notice of parliament." He is given the widest powers.
There is further comment on that actual provision in the auditor general's report of 1943. In 1943 we went one step farther. It was found that, with the enormous increase in government departments and spending, the auditor general's staff was spending much too much time in checking on petty accounts and duplicating the work already done by internal audits. Therefore there was a further change agreed upon by the auditor general, the deputy minister and the comptroller general. The present Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley) was then Minister of Finance, and he referred to the matter in the house in 1942, as reported at page 5082 of Hansard, as follows:
Our desire was to draw from all possible sources lessons and suggestions as to the best possible way in which to present to parliament the information necessary to enable it to exercise wisely and efficiently its control over financial matters and assure itself that the executive arm of government is properly carrying out its stewardship.
That, to my mind, summarizes very well the responsibility of the auditor general to this parliament. We only have to compare the reports of the auditor general from 1943 on with the previous reports to realize how that lightened the burden of petty detail and gave the auditor general the opportunity of doing the splendid job he now does.
I have traced this development to show how the position has grown in power and responsibility. The people of this country do entrust us with the public funds. We in turn entrust them to the government of the day, and the auditor general is our watchdog to assure us, the members of the House of Commons, that the money which we have voted for appropriations is properly spent.
Since the Canadian National Railway involves the expenditure of public funds-last week, for example, we voted another S8,960,000 to make up the deficit of the Canadian National Railways-it is my submission that we should have the auditor general, our auditor, report on the Canadian National Railways.
My next point was the fact that the auditor general can do this. There seems to be some question whether or not he or his department is capable of doing the audit of the Canadian National Railways. There was a time when the department of the auditor general was very small. The national budget was small; his department was small. They were engaged mostly in routine matters. But in the last ten years there has been a great increase in

C.N.R.-Appointment of Auditors
the status of the auditor general, in the staff and in the qualities of the staff. I need only remind the house that two years ago the auditor general audited a $6 'billion budget of this house. I need only read the list of the crown companies which he audited in his last report to show the scope of his audits as far as business is concerned. They are as follows: Aero Timber Products Limited; Allied War Supplies Corporation; Board of Grain Commissioners; Canadian Arsenals Limited; Canadian Broadcasting Corporation; Canadian Wool Board Limited; Citadel Merchandising Limited; Commodity Prices Stabilization Limited; Eldorado Mining and Refining (1944) Limited; Exports Credits Insurance Corporation; Federal Aircraft Limited; Federal District Commission; Foreign Exchange Control Board; Inspection Board of United Kingdom and Canada; Melbourne Merchandising Limited; National Battlefields Commission:	National Harbours Board;
National Railways Munitions Limited; Northern Transportation Company Limited; Park Steamship Company Limited; Polymer Corporation Limited; Research Enterprises Limited; Small Arms Limited; Sorel Gun Plant; Sugar Administrator; Turbo Research Limited; Veterans Housing Project (Ottawa) Limited; Veterans Housing Project (Toronto) Limited; Victory Aircraft Limited; War Assets Corporation; War Supplies Limited; Wartime Food Corporation Limited; Wartime Housing Limited; Wartime Metals Corporation; Wartime Shipbuilding Limited and the Yukon Council, together with many other smaller government agencies. When you read that list it is Obvious that the auditor general must have the staff and the knowledge to perform an audit of the Canadian National Railways.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OP GEORGE A. TOUCHE AND COMPANY AS AUDITORS
speechtext: That is why taxes were so high.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OP GEORGE A. TOUCHE AND COMPANY AS AUDITORS
speechtext:
I shall deal with that in just a moment. The auditor general audits all public expenditures and crown companies execpt the Canadian National Railways and the Trans-Canada Air Lines; therefore the actual bigness need not dismay us. Last year, for example, the Canadian National Railways had a revenue of $434 million and operating expenses of $305 million, a business which was very small in comparison with other public expenditures audited by the auditor general.
Let us turn and see how the firm of George A. Touche and Company does this audit. After the revision of the Canadian National Railway Act in 1933 by the Bennett government, an excellent internal audit was set up
within the Canadian National Railways, and what the auditing firm of George A. Touche and Company did wras what any auditing firm would do under such circumstances. They turned a flock of juniors loose to take a spot-check on the internal audit of the Canadian National Railways auditors, and then the material was correlated by the heads of the Touche Company in this report. I have been unable to find the cost, but I shall ask that question later. In 1934, the cost was $50,000 plus undetermined expenses. I submit, therefore, that the auditor general could certainly do the job.
My third point is the most important one. I feel that the auditor general could not only do the job but do a much better job. First, let us examine the report of George A. Touche and Company. I doubt whether there is one member in twenty who has read it through. I know, after seven years in parliament, that this is the first one I have ever read through and, after having read it through, I must confess I was not much wiser than when I started. It is a proper business report such as would be made to any big corporation; it is lacking in detail, and throughout it all we have the feeling that anything which is legal is quite proper so far as the firm of George A. Touche and Company is concerned. They are not going to question policy. Compare that with the auditor general's report, one part of which is a proper business report, and then the other part of comments which I think every member of parliament reads and studies; certainly a great number use it as the source of speeches. Look at his critical comment, very fair and open and complete comment on all government expenditures. In every way there is full detail given, going far beyond the actual routine of figures and presented in a form we can digest. More than that, the auditor general is able to bring to parliament the things in which hon. members are interested. It is not hard to find the reason for this. To begin with, the auditor general is the servant of parliament. He is in touch with parliament. The second thing I find is that Hansard is compulsory reading for each of the different audit supervisors in his department. So that not only when they come to the audit do they know what they are auditing, but they have some idea in the backs of their minds of the desire of parliament which prompted the legislation and the appropriation. They know, too, of matters which are of special interest to members of parliament, and their attention is directed to these matters when they do the audit. I shall give an example of that. We know that since the end of the war there has

C.N.R.-Appointment oj Auditors
been considerable discussion of pensions, and service pensions in particular. I refer to page 26 of the auditor general's report of this matter on which he comments. He has audited militia pensions, and he has commented on a pension paid to an admiral in the north Atlantic. He says:
The computations for pension are certified as correct, subject to the following qualification.
My argument is that a civilian auditor would end there. The pension is calculated on the man's pay and retirement, and the calculation was correct. But the auditor general knows the attention which is paid in parliament to these pensions. So he went behind the figures to see how they were built up, and he found a shabby thing. He found that this admiral commanding, who had left the command in May, when he went on retirement leave in September had himself posted back on command at command rates of pay, although doing nothing, thus receiving an extra $4.50 a day for six months of retirement leave and thus, because of his pay having been swollen up in that way, henceforth he would receive from the people of Canada $509 more in his pension annually than he would be entitled to except for this action on his part. The auditor general comments upon that and properly so, as not being within the intent of parliament when it passed the Militia Pension Act, and no doubt when the Minister of National Defence brings his estimates before the house the soldier members will have something to say on the question.
The auditor general's report abounds in things like that, On the previous page there is something in connection with housing. There have been long discussions in this house on this question. Indeed, there is no subject which has occupied the attention of parliament more than the question of housing, and the auditor comments on a number of matters, some of them raised by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) with respect to the improper expenditures of funds in connection with housing. Many cases are covered by the auditor general in his report.
Last year I had a resolution on the order paper for some time with reference to the question of crown taxation, my feeling being that the crown should pay municipal taxes. I am concerned about this, because there is in my riding a city which is very hard hit. The auditor general found, on going through the reports, that a great number of crown companies made payments to municipalities in lieu of taxes, and he properly pointed out, for the information of members of parliament,
IMr. J. Sinclair.]
men such as myself, that this was, to all intents and purposes, payment of municipal taxes. He did not comment upon it, but he called attention to the fact that the crown was actually, by this method, paying taxes in certain instances on crown land, without acknowledging the principle everywhere, a thing which I certainly intend to discuss when my resolution comes up, if it ever does see the light of day.
There are other good uses of the auditor general. For example, there is the comparison of salary scales, since he is the one man who can check all departments of government and see whether each department follows the same procedure in the payment of salaries. There is great value in consistency.
In my own service in the air force we always felt that we were in a preferred class receiving better pay, better treatment, billets, transportation and so forth. I mentioned this in the conscription debates, when I pointed out that it was unfair to the army and the navy to have such a situation existing, and urged that they should be brought up to our level. So in the civil service there is also a feeling of resentment if one branch is treated better than another. I say therefore that the auditor general, by his searching comments on all branches, exercises an excellent effect.
I need only refer to the annual report on salaries. One or two examples close to parliament have been turned up by the auditor general. For instance, there is the payment to John Grierson of expenses after he had left the film board, and the payment of expenses to judges' wives while the judges were on duty in Ottawa. These matters were properly drawn to the attention of parliament. In the latter instance, what had been done was legal in that the government had authorized the payment, A civilian auditor would have gone no farther than that; but the auditor general, our servant, knowing our attitude on the question, drew attention to it. The firm of George A. Touche and Company cannot do that. The only Hansard that will be read by the firm of George A. Touche and Company for some time to come will be this Hansard. Such a firm, I maintain, has not the knowledge of other departments which the auditor general has, nor does it know the conditions as members of parliament do, who are the trustees of the public.
The best test that I can put to the House of Commons is the comparison between these two reports. One member in twenty may have read the report of the Canadian National, but every member without exception has read the last part of the comments of the auditor

C.N.R.-Appointment of Auditors
general on the public funds of Canada. There was an interesting confirmation of this last week in the freight rates inquiry, when Colonel Ralston, a member of this house for many years, and at one time minister of finance, complained that he could not get necessary information with respect to the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific railways from their reports.
The auditor general can also be called on at any time-for extra information by any member of parliament during the session, not as in the case of Touche and Company, only before the railway committee.
I have another and far better and deeper reason for the contention that the auditor general can make a better report than any civilian auditor, and that is his independence. Once appointed under the great seal of Canada, he is responsible only to parliament. He can feel as free as he likes to make criticism of what he thinks is wrong, and it would take a very great dereliction of duty on his part for both houses of parliament to pass an address requiring his removal. Because of that independence, he can make the sort of reports he has made for the last four or five years.
Compare that with the appointment of a civilian auditor by act of parliament-not by resolution of parliament but by act of parliament. He must be very grateful to the government of the day for that appointment. I of course, as a supporter of this government, have every confidence that the present civilian auditor appointed by the government is doing a responsible job. But if the time ever comes, and it may, when I sit over there in opposition, and a Conservative government appoints another auditor, or a C.C.F. government appoints one, I might not have the same confidence in that auditor. The auditor of public accounts should be like Caesar's wife, above reproach.
Having perhaps a suspicious mind, I thought I would look up the record, because I was quite sure that when the Tories were in power they did not employ this firm of Touche and Company, and so I turned to the first appointment in 1934. I was disappointed because I found that Touche and Company were the first auditors appointed by act of parliament to be auditors of the Canadian National Railways in the time of the Bennett administration. That was when Doctor Manion made such a glowing reference to the abilities of this firm, which I said I would read in fairness to the company. Doctor Manion's remarks are to be found in Hansard of 1934 as follows:
It has been decided, after a good deal of consideration, that the auditors who have been
doing the work for a good many years-I do not know exactly how long, but eight or ten years at any rate-are so well trained in the work and are so capable that it would be wise to appoint them at least for this year. I am informed by the railway people themselves that it would take quite a long time for any group of auditors to learn the method of auditing such an immense system of books and accounts as are contained in this vast business.
It was a vast business by the standards of those days, but small compared with public business today.
Tor example, I am told that there are no other chartered accountants in Canada who are familiar with the interstate commerce commission's type of accounting, and the accounting of the Canadian National Railways is carried on under the same rules as those of the interstate commerce commission for the railways of the United States.
The manner of this appointment, however, was challenged, and I was delighted to find that my own leader, at that time leader of the opposition, suggested that it was not proper to have the government of the day make the appointment by act of parliament. He suggested that it should be done by resolution of both houses. Quite casually I looked ahead to the 1935 debate and, to my surprise I found that the Conservative government in 1935 had dispensed with indispensable George A. Touche and had appointed a new firm known as Clarkson, Gordon, Dilworth, Guilfoyle and Nash. There was a touch of humour on that occasion, because one member suggested that in the broken-down condition of the Canadian National at that time it was doubtful whether the railway could carry all that as one load. The charge was made by the opposition-and there was a long and bitter debate-that the firm of George A. Touche and Company had been removed because they had been too critical in the report submitted. They had criticized the debt financing of the Canadian National Railways. The charge was taken up by the national press of Canada. Doctor Manion answered it by saying that he thought a great deal of the agitation had been started by the firm of George A. Touche and Company themselves because they were angry at losing this valuable contract.
Doctor Manion was reminded about the glowing recommendation he had made in the previous year and was asked by members whether the firm of George A. Touche and Company had not been satisfactory, had not been efficient, but he pointed out that that was not the issue at all. He said that the appointment was for one year and that the question was not one of dismissal but of change. When finally challenged, he said

C.N.R.-Appointment of Auditors
something, one sentence which I think is pregnant with meaning, so much so that I will read it. I cannot find it at the moment, but he said that he did not doubt that the firm was satisfactory but that, and I quote, "The firm of Clarkson, Gordon, Dilworth, Guil-foyle and Nash would be more satisfactory," more satisfactory, of course, to the government of the day.
That brings home to me more than anything else the dependence of an auditor appointed in such fashion. Naturally an auditor so appointed will be grateful to the government supporting it and would not be likely to make embarrassing comment. The significant thing about this is that the next year we find, with the Liberals in power, that George A. Touche is back. The significant thing about it is that there was no question at that time of the right of the government to change auditors. That precedent had been established the previous year, so no explanation was now necessary. But once again it is interesting to see how consistent the opposition was, despite the change in membership. At this time R. B. Bennett, as leader of the opposition, got up and said he thought this should not be done by act of parliament, but should be done by resolution of both houses. That is why I take the stand that, because of this complete independence from the government of the day, our auditor general can do a better job, a freer job, than any firm of civilian auditors whose appointment is made by an act of parliament sponsored by the government of the day. Because of that, I think the best comparison again is for members to read the two reports. It is also significant that the firm of George A. Touche and Company have never again been as critical in their reports as they were in that one unfortunate year of 1935, on which they lost the job.
I wish to revert to this debate of 1934, because nowhere in that debate was the suggestion made that the auditor general do the job. Why was that? There were two reasons which I thought appeared in the debate. The first was that there was great political sensitivity, if I may use that phrase, at that time over political interference with the management of the Canadian National Railways. The Canadian National Railway Act had been passed, and it was hoped to have the railway completely removed from any political control. Undoubtedly there wras the feeling that, by having an ordinary civilian firm of auditors do the job, that objective might be strengthened. The second thing was that I do not think the auditor general's department of that day were capable of doing the job. After all,

the Canadian National at that time was almost as big business as the government. More than that, the auditor general's department had no opportunity to do business audits as they have now. That situation, of course, has changed greatly since that time. The enormous wartime budgets of the government, the multitude of crown companies and other agencies which the auditor general does audit, have given him and his department that experience. Part of that is also because of the character of the man who is now auditor general, Mr. Watson Sellar. He was originally with the Department of Finance; for ten years he was comptroller general of Canada; and when he came to the department of the auditor general in 1940, as auditor general, he made great improvements throughout the branch in the quality of the staff, in the work, and in the type of report presented. Perhaps the greatest tribute to the staff is the fact that private industry and crown companies have steadily robbed his staff of keymen by paying them two or three times the wages they get as chartered accountants with the auditor general's department.
