speechtext: Where did they go? Did they go to private accounting firms? Did these expert men who had been trained in the auditor general's department go to private auditing firms?

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OP GEORGE A. TOUCHE AND COMPANY AS AUDITORS
speechtext: Not to private accounting firms, but to private industry and as comptrollers of crown companies.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OP GEORGE A. TOUCHE AND COMPANY AS AUDITORS
speechtext: Is the hon. member sure they did not go to private accounting firms?

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OP GEORGE A. TOUCHE AND COMPANY AS AUDITORS
speechtext:
They may go to private accounting firms, because the training they get here is training which cannot be equalled anywhere else. The robbery which I resent the most is the crown companies taking them from the auditor general's department and paying them $7,000 and $8,000 in two cases for auditing jobs and comptroller jobs with these crown companies, salaries which the auditor general's department cannot equal. But here I think a tribute should be paid to the men who stayed with the auditor general's department, despite these attractions; and one of the reasons they stayed was undoubtedly the esprit de corps built up in that department by our present auditor general, Watson Sellar. Perhaps, as one last tribute to him, I might say that two days age I telephoned to Mr. Sellar about this matter and I found that he was absent in New York. He is now, I suppose the phrase could be used, auditor general for the united nations. Until

C.N.R.-Appointment oj Auditors
1950 he is senior of the three auditors appointed to audit the accounts of the united nations, which is certainly another tribute to the ability of the man.
Aside from those arguments, there is one last argument which I should like to make because I am a Liberal-, not a socialist. This matter of crown companies is coming very much to the fore in the development of government here in Canada. Certainly one of the reasons why the auditor general was not suggested in 1933 was that crown companies were unheard of then. We got the Canadian National Railways by accident. It was forced on us through the collapse of the Canadian Northern and the Grand Trunk. The words "crown company" were not used at that time., but now we are in this crown company business very heavily.
I have one or two observations to make on these crown companies. I do not object to crown companies as such I think they have a rightful field in natural public monopolies. I also think there is no reason why the crown should not go into competitive private enterprise, and I use that word "competitive" because I do not believe they should move in a field in which free competition exists and monopolize it to themselves. For example, I see no reason why the C.C.F. government should not go into the slaughterhouse business or the brick business in Saskatchewan, with, however, these reservations. First of all, they must continue free competition against the people who are in that business themselves; and, second, they must pay the full taxes which every other company in competition with them must pay. The argument is, of course, that for a federal company to pay federal taxes is just taking money from this pocket and putting it in that pocket. But when that is done, however, and an audited statement is submitted, the people of Canada are able to see whether or not this company is efficient and whether it can stand on its own feet as compared with private competition which pays the same taxes. Certainly when it comes to provincial and municipal taxes of a federal crown company, they certainly are doubly obligated to pay them rather than to take advantage of the provincial and municipal taxpayers in one community of the country in order to build up an unnatural balance sheet.
The second point is that these crown companies must be responsible to parliament. It is not a matter of political control. Certainly it would be difficult for a crown company to compete with private industry if there was political patronage all through the crown company. But since these crown companies are started with and employ public funds, and since those which are not successful come back to parliament for more public funds, as the Canadian National did this year, it is most important that this parliament should have control over crown companies in that respect. It is quite true that in all of the crown companies 'but the Canadian National and Trans-Canada Air Lines we do have that control. One obvious suggestion which I make is to have the auditor general do them all.
But more than that is needed. There must be, in this parliament, some item in the estimates under which each crown company could be discussed. I suggest-and my colleague, the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) mentioned this-that, if needs be. an item of $10 could appear in the estimates of each minister responsible for crown companies. The hon. member for Quebec South suggested that the $10 could be spent if needs be, if the company does not need the money, on a big picture of the House of Commons, to be hung in the head office with the title "Our Bosses"; and in the present state I would say "Our Bosses" question mark. Then perhaps these crown companies would realize that the parliament of Canada in the end is being held responsible 'by the people of Canada for what they are doing. They are not in the position of private companies who must report directly back to their shareholders, to the people who put up the money. The route is too long, from the taxpayer of Canada, through the House of Commons, through the government to the crown companies to have that feeling of responsibilitj'. That feeling of responsibility would come, however, if somewhere in the estimates each year there were an item under which the conduct of each crown company could be discussed, and if as the basis of discussion, we had the full report of our own auditor general on that subject. That is why I feel this bill should not pass in its present form. I feel that the work started by William Lyon Mackenzie in 1835, with his report on grievances to bring not only the appropriation of all public funds into parliament's hands but also the accounting of those appropriations into parliament's hands, should be completed by the inclusion of this last crown company within the scope of the auditor general.
If this bill is put to a vote immediately I will vote against it, because I feel I have shown that the auditor general is certainly the proper person to do the work, and I have demonstrated, at least to my own satisfaction, that he can do a better job. These things, however, are open to discussion, so I suggest to the minister that, instead of this bill being

C.N.R.-Appointment of Auditors
referred to the committee of the whole house after second reading, it be referred to the railway committee, and that the railway committee summon before it the auditor general and the firm of George A. Touche and Company, if needs be, and there settle whether or not the auditor general of Canada, who certainly should do the job, can do it. Therefore, if the minister gives the assurance that this will be done I -will vote for second reading. Otherwise I will vote against the second reading and make that motion when we get into committee.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OP GEORGE A. TOUCHE AND COMPANY AS AUDITORS
speechtext:
I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair) on the excellent speech he has delivered. I feel sure that hon. members in all sections of the house will support the hon. gentleman, in view of the fact that the adoption of his recommendation would save the taxpayers of this country a considerable sum of money. I believe those who are familiar with the operations of the Canadian National Railways in recent years will agree that the accounting system has been maintained in satisfactory fashion. Mr. Cooper, the vice-president, who is also the comptroller, has taken a keen interest in presenting each year a balance sheet as favourable as possible, and I am sure all the directors have been concerned about making this publicly owned railway as efficient as possible. Last year, when the committee was meeting, I noticed in the balance sheet an item of some $12,000,000 on the asset side in connection with insurance. When I questioned Mr. Cooper regarding this item he mentioned that at the time of the amalgamation they took over some insurance funds to the extent of about $1,500,000. Then they decided that, rather than pay out premiums to privately operated companies to carry risks on stations here, there and everywhere across the country, there was no reason why the Canadian National should not set up its own insurance fund. However they charged the prevailing rates, and by 1930 had built up a surplus of about $10,000,000. Then they reduced their premiums by $1,000,000 a year, and a year or so later found that it was unnecessary to charge any premiums at all. So, for some fifteen years the Canadian National Railways have been able to provide for all their losses resulting from fire out of the interest on the accumulated amount that has been built up.
I submit that if the accounts of this corporation had been audited throughout the years by a firm like George A. Touche and Company, they probably would not have given any attention to the payment of high

premiums each year to privately operated insurance companies. There would not have been anything irregular about it; but since the directors of the Canadian National have the interests of the public at heart, they are concerned about economies of this kind.
Last year, when the committee met, the president presented us with a memorandum in connection with the operations of the Canada-West Indies Steamships branch of the company. Mr. Vaughan pointed out that the company was incorporated in 1927, to implement the Canada-West Indies trade agreement of July 6, 1925. Under the first agreement of 1912, the Royal Mail Steam Packet Company had operated four ships on a fortnightly service between Canada and the eastern group of islands, for which the company was paid an annual subsidy of $340,000. In the 1920 agreement, Canada also undertook to provide a service to the western group of islands, and this service was assigned to the Canadian government merchant marine. The memorandum mentioned the amount asked by privately owned corporations for this service. The Royal Mail Steam Packet Company put in a tender for a fortnightly mail, passenger and freight service with four new 12-knot passenger vessels, in accordance with the trade agreement, for which they asked an annual subsidy of $582,000. They also offered to perform the sei'vice every twelve days with smaller ships for an annual subsidy of $534,000. An agreement w'as not reached, however, with this company. The Canadian National Railways went into this field, but for some reason or another-perhaps it was the change of government which occurred in 1930-the subsidies which previously had been paid privately owned companies were not made available to the publicly owned company, and as a result this operation was not profitable. The balance sheet- of the company at the end of 1945 show's that for the whole period of operation there has been an over-all loss of $4,983,000. The statement, however, goes on to say that the balance sheet is not necessarily a final summation of all the gains or losses resultant from the operation of this service. The president explained that it was not unreasonable that the Canadian National might have been compensated on a basis similar to that under which the privately owned company would have been compensated if they had performed the service.
In the committee the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) reviewed this matter in some detail, and made what I think everyone would agree was a very fair and reasonable case. Later, a motion was pre-

sented to the committee by the hon. member and myself with a view to giving the Canadian National Steamships relief from this deficit of 85,000,000 which had accumulated through the years, but we were not successful in getting a majority of the committee to agree to recommend that the government take some action which would relieve the Canadian National of this item. When Mr. Matthews, who represented George A. Touche and Company, was before the committee I asked some questions regarding what would be his personal opinion concerning the carrying of this item in the balance sheet of the Canadian National for fifteen years or more. He replied:
I would not consider that would be part of our function. I think it is a matter of government policy, and our job we regard to be the setting out of facts. As long as the Department of Finance regard it as a liability, we have no alternative.
I asked whether he would make some comments if he were auditing for a privately owned corporation. The hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Jackman) came to my assistance and said:
May I ask this question of Mr. Matthews? Are there many companies which your firm audits, and with which you are familiar, where a deficit has been carried for fifteen years or more and interest has accrued each year and piled up there?
Mr. Matthews:	No.
Mr. Jackman:	Do you know of any?
Mr. Matthews:	No. It is in the same category as the Canadian National railway system was in 1937 when the Capital Revision Act was brought in; the same principle.
Then the minister said:
Do you audit any other railway company besides the national system?
Mr. Matthews:	Not in Canada. But we regard that as a matter of policy outside our function. Our job is to set out facts to the committee and not matters of policy.
Mr. Nicholson:	I appreciate that very much.
But if you were auditing for a private company, would you not have some comment to make?
Mr. Matthews:	If we were auditing a commercial corporation with a deficit of $5,000,000 and which owed the bank or anyone else the same amount, that would be set out in the balance sheet as it is in the case of the West Indies steamships; and it would again be a matter of corporate policy as to reorganization.
Mr. Nicholson:	Would you not have some
comment to make regarding the carrying on of this for fifteen years?
Hon. Mr. Chevrier: Has not that matter been disposed of pretty much by the committee?
Mr. Nicholson:	I think it is quite relevant.
I wish to contrast the position of George A. Touche and Company with regard to a matter of that sort with the comments made by the auditor general in connection with the operation of crown companies, and of several
departments. I agree entirely with the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair) that this sort of statement by George A. Touche and Company is quite unsatisfactory when compared with the statement made by the auditor general regarding the year's operations.
Several ministers of the crown have been embarrassed by remarks made by the auditor general. Apparently George A. Touche and Company remembered vividly what happened while the Bennett government was in office and when they made some comments regarding matters which I think come within the purview of the auditors' administration. I have been reading Hansard, and I find in Hansard of February' 22, 1935, at page 1092, there is reported a speech by Mr. Manion, in which he referred to an article which had appeared in the Toronto Star. That article reads:
Far from welcoming the proposal of the auditors that the grossly inflated debt of the Canadian National Railways be pared down the Bennett government is demanding that the auditors be dismissed.
The explanation that will be given for the proposed dismissal of the auditors no doubt will be that the firm has its headquarters in England, but so it had a year ago when Mr. Bennett and Dr. Manion were loud in praise of its work.
Apparently a firm such as George A. Touche and Company run a certain risk when they make comments regarding a problem as important to the Canadian people as the inflated debt of the Canadian National Railways. I submit that it would be in the best interests of the Canadian National Railways, and certainly it would be in the best interests of the taxpayers of Canada if the auditing of the financial position of the Canadian National Railways was carried out, as the hon. member for Vancouver North has suggested, by the auditor general.
In the last report which the auditor general submitted to parliament, he makes mention of some matters which hon. members of the opposition are certainly going to use before this session is over. On page 22 there is reference to vote 426, which refers to some tenders which were invited by the director of the Veterans Land Act for the construction of nine houses at Boueherville, Quebec. Bids ranging from $45,884 to $70,200 were rejected as excessive and then, later on in the paragraph, it is stated:
In the fiscal year $87,018.10 war paid by way of progress payments. Administrative officers advise that this contract is under investigation; consequently the payments have been accepted in the audit subject to that qualification. Further claims of $103,820.85 with respect to the contract were, at the time of audit, in the department.

I think any auditor who will embarrass the administration by putting down in black and white details in connection with tenders being rejected because bids ranging from $45,884 to $70,200 were rejected as excessive when actual vouchers in excess of $190,000 have been taken in is a pretty satisfactory auditor for the Canadian National Railways. Then on page 24 reference is made to the director of housing being retired with three months' retiring leave as of March 1. The position was abolished and he was given an annual allowance of $1,174. As of that date he was fifty years of age with ten years' service. I am sure my deskmate, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, (Mr. Knowles) is going to have something to say about an order in council that provides a pension of $100 a month for life for a man fifty years of age when we cannot get legislation before parliament to do more for our old age pensioners than we have up to date.
Another reference on page 29 is to the de Havilland contract for $6,445,025, representing shipments made to various R.A.F. and R.C.A.F. depots. He states:
Proof of delivery was established by the records for invoices approximating $1,000,000, but no proof of delivery on the balance was produced in the course of audit.
There we have a matter of $5,500,000 which apparently was not accounted for to the satisfaction of the auditor general. I am sure that all members of parliament realize that is the sort of audit we require rather than the type of audit carried out by George A. Touche and Company, although I agree with the hon. member for Vancouver North that this is a well recognized and reliable firm, and I have no quarrel with Mr. Matthews who has been before our committee for several years.
In conclusion, I should like to move an amendment along the lines of the argument advanced by the hon. member for Vancouver North, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. I should like to draw your attention, Mr. Speaker, to page 228 of Beauchesne, third edition, citation 657, which I think is my authority for moving the following amendment:
That all the words after "that" be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"this bill be not now read a second time but that it be resolved that in the opinion of this house the government should give consideration to the making of provision for the auditing of the accounts of the Canadian National Railways to be done by the auditor general of Canada.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OP GEORGE A. TOUCHE AND COMPANY AS AUDITORS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as one of those who during the last war urged in the province of Ontario that the

government of the day should take over this system, I wish to say a few words tonight. I addressed meetings along with the late Sir Adam Beck, but we found very few supporters of our policy to nationalize the Canadian National Railways and its various subsidies. After a success had been made of public ownership and the provision of cheap light and power in Ontario, we addressed meetings at St. Thomas, London, Kingston, Belleville and many other points in the province.
The component parts of the road were taken over to form what is now known as the Canadian National Railways. The mistakes of private ownership had been apparent for many years prior to that. There was evident useless duplication and waste, and the result was that a royal commission was appointed, known as the Drayton-Smith-Aeworth commission. This was made up of Mr. Smith, the president of the New York Central railroad; Mr. Acworth, a prominent British engineer and Sir Henry Drayton, then chairman of the board of railway commissioners, now known as the board of transport commissioners.
As a public ownership man, I have always taken a consistent stand in connection with this railroad, and I wish to compliment the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair) on the splendid address he has given tonight in support of what I have proposed ever since I have been a member of the house, namely, that we have our own auditor general as an independent audit. The bill recommends that the Touche chartered accountants be appointed as independent auditors for the year 1947 to make a continuous audit of the accounts of national railways as defined in the act. The auditor general is an independent auditor because he does not take work from other private business concerns, the way some of these auditing firms do.
The auditor general is the auditor of public ownership in general; he is the auditor of all the departments of this government. We have had some very good men in this position. I believe a public ownership venture should be administered by those who believe in public ownership. I cannot find one person on the board of directors, either past or present, who has been well known as a supporter of the principle of public ownership. In Ontario we had experience with private companies in the providing of light and power and the hydro system as a public venture was begun after 1905. The hydro started and took over the remaining water powers of the Niagara river and reduced the costs to domestic and commercial users of light and power to one-third.

C.N.R.-Appointment of Auditors
I believe the time has come when a change should be made in the practice of appointing auditors for the Canadian National Railways. Last week the directors of the railways made a report to parliament in which they estimated the deficit for 1946 at nearly $9,000,000, and an item of $8,961,570 appears in the supplementary estimates to make up that deficit. But the annual report of the railways is not out yet. The appointment of private auditors is a violation of the recommendations which were made in the Drayton-Aeworth report after an investigation which cost this country a huge sum of money. They reported that there was duplication and waste all over the country in the construction of branch lines and in other ways which cost a huge expenditure of money and they recommended that no new ventures or new lines be started without the recommendation of the railway commission from the commercial aspect. That report has not since been implemented at all by this house.
The scope of the audit made by George A. Touche and Company is set out on pages 6 and 7 of their report to parliament for the year ended December 31, 1945, the last report made by this company. The system includes the Canadian National Railways Securities Trust, the Canadian National (West Indies) Steamships, Limited, and the Trans-Canada Air Lines. I believe that the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair) is quite right in proposing that we should substitute the auditor general to audit the Canadian National Railways system. Under the old act, from 1924 on, it was the board of directors of the railways who appointed the auditors. The act vyas amended in 1932 requiring an address from both houses of parliament to appoint an auditor for the system. The auditors have failed to make any recommendations for improving the efficiency of the system. After all is said and done, the railway in part is not run from the commercial aspect. In the first two and a half years of world war II the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian Nat.onal Railways made more money than they made in the whole period of the first great war. A return was made to the house, showing that down to the end of 1941 one of these railway systems made $27,000,000 and the other, $25,500,000 more than it made during the whole of the first world war. In addition to the railway itself, there are the hotel services, the land and ocean services and now the Trans-Canada Air Lines, and the expenditures of the system are going up by leaps and bounds. The road is not run from the commercial aspect. Its headquarters
never should have been transferred to Montreal, and money should never have been wasted on that hole in Montreal. There has been useless duplication and waste in the hotel system. In towns where there was business for only one hotel the railway insisted on building another, even though the materials were wanted for building small houses all across the country.
Furthermore, there has been no proper inspection or control of the United States subsidiaries of this railway system. In Ontario the railway makes more money than in any other part of its system, yet the province of Ontario has been completely ignored in connection with betterments, its requirements of rolling stock, locomotives, box cars and things like that. But the railway is spending money on its United States subsidiaries. It gets rolling stock, passenger trains and other equipment for its subsidiaries in the United States. Charity should begin at home.
I believe that the directors do not direct. The directors are appointed from one political party.
Again I believe that the free transportation system should be revised. I am not referring to anybody connected with the government or to members of either house of parliament; far from it. But I say that the railway commission does not supervise properly that particular branch, with the result that we are not getting the revenue we should get from the operation of this railway.
I am a real public ownership man myself, and public ownership must succeed. I believe that we have a faithful able president and faithful officers and rank and file working for the system. They have worked hard at small pay and a large majority of them are efficient, but in some cases in the past exorbitant pensions have been paid to retired officials, and parliament has lost all control over the system. When you ask questions in the house about it you cannot get an answer but are told to go to some committee which was appointed, and largely whitewash the operations of the system. In the report you find very little about the workings of the system. I will give one example. They brought up from the maritime provinces to Toronto an old tub, which is known as the Northumberland and now runs between Toronto and Port Dalhousie. It is not fit for lake traffic. The boat has been condemned. The predecessor of the minister wrote me a letter about it. My hon. friend the member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) had a picnic on this boat; and at times it got stuck out in the lake. It is a wonder he ever got home. What was not good enough twenty years ago for Prince

Edward Island is shipped up to Toronto; an old tub not fit to run down there is good enough for Toronto, a public ownership city. Yet they can afford to spend $2,500,000 at Sorel for a new car fern- for Prince Edward Island.

When it gets up to $5,000,000 it is beyond me. When the railway is dealing in these astronomical figures money is much more likely to be wasted. I am not complaining about Prince Edward Island getting its due in public ownership, because I have been a real genuine public ownership man all my life. We should have some known public ownership directors on this board instead of some of those who are appointed for political purposes. I am not saying that we do not do this when our party is in power, but if we are to have efficient administration of a large publicly-owned utility, particularly with the expansion that is going on, we must use some degree of economy and run the road as a commercial proposition.
I believe that the auditor general, who is now making an elaborate report to parliament on our own departments, should be appointed to audit this system. We have had the experience in Ontario of large expenditures on publicly owned light and power. The city auditor of our city inspects the system daily, inspects the large taxpayer, the Consumers Gas Company and all the other activities of the system. The auditor general has a very fine department now. and he should be appointed to audit this system and make a study of the various proposals which have been made. The scope of the audit should be enlarged, instead of being simply a check-up of the system, an examination of major expenditures and audit tests as set out on page 6 of the Touche report for 1945. It is just a test audit that is made, not a daily audit of each office, but just a test audit here and there. It puts me in mind of a Gallup poll. They have a few people meet in an office, and they size up by such tests how the country is going. It is the same here. It is just a test audit. They pick out a piece here and there. You will find it all on page 6:
(a)	Examination of major expenditure authorities in conjunction with the recorded resolutions of the directors, which in turn are related to corporate by-laws, orders in council and acts of parliament;
(b)	audit tests in the offices of regions, separately operated properties and system headquarters, limited to a cross-section of the major expenditures so authorized:
(c)	Examination into the adequacy of the interna] audit control in general as exercised by the accounting staff of the system. In this eon-
JMr. Church.]
nection we work in collaboration with the executive accounting officers at headquarters having as a common objective the securing of maximum internal protection to the system iu the control of cash receipts and expenditures, securities held, material stores, accounts receivable, et cetera, and through the carrying of fidelity bond insurance with outside underwriters, and , . .
Then we come to the securities trusts and the other systems, but I shall not continue reading it any further. I believe the time has come, as I said in my opening remarks, when the auditor general should have control over all these outside boards. We would get better results in the work which has to be done.
In conclusion, may I say I believe that, ever since the start, the system has had big eyes in building branch lines. They built duplicating branch lines all over the country. A great many of them had to be ripped up and scrapped because their development has been a waste. The road was not run in a commercial way, and there has been duplication of branch lines, to which I have already referred. In the interests of the country, in the interests of the system and in the interests of getting some efficiency in the system I believe that the auditor general of Canada should audit the accounts. It should not be an official auditor who is described in the bill as an independent auditor. He is not an independent auditor at all, because he is doing work for other privately owned agencies.

speechtext:
I rise to support the remarks made by the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair). In my opinion, the house is indebted to him for an informing and instructive speech, one of those speeches which will be well worth reading tomorrow in Hansard. I am quite sure, Mr. Speaker, that his native ability, his academic training, his parliamentary and administrative experience, and shall I say his British Columbia environment, fitted him well to make a speech such as he made this evening. I think it was one of the most, lucid and informative speeches that I have heard in the house this session.
I was particularly interested in the fact that the hon. member for Vancouver North gave us a clear historical review of the situation. He then made his criticism and, in addition to that, put forward his suggestions and his constructive proposals. That is what I consider as evidence of a worth-while debate. I was very much interested in the illustrations he gave to us this evening of the deficiencies of the present system of auditing. As a relatively new member of the house, I must say that I was greatly informed this evening. I

C.N.R.-Appointment of Auditors
learned a lot from the speech of the hon. member for Vancouver North. I am not going to repeat any of the things he said; the hour is getting late. I wish to say that, as a result of listening to the speech of the hon. member for Vancouver North, I realize now the great importance of what appeared on the surface to be a rather unimportant bill, and I urge other hon. members to give support to his proposals. Because of his arguments and the illustrations he gave this evening, I for one extend the strongest support to his .suggestion that this bill be sent to the railway committee for further consideration before receiving third reading.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OP GEORGE A. TOUCHE AND COMPANY AS AUDITORS
speechtext:
The bill which is before the house at the present time is an annual bill dealing with the appointment of auditors for the Canadian National Railways. It is not a new bill. The form in which it is now is not at all different from the form in which it has appeared in previous years. In fact, ever since 1932 the manner of appointing auditors for the national railway has been the same in effect as the bill which is now before the house.
This year the bill seeks to appoint the same firm of auditors, namely George A. Touche and Company of Toronto and Montreal, to make a continuous audit under the provision of the Canadian National-Canadian Pacific Act. That act deals with the manner in which auditors shall be appointed and sets out that the auditors shall be appointed by resolution of parliament.
The hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair) dealt with the resolution stage and suggested that it should be done in that manner now. To my mind, there is no difference in the suggestion made by the hon. gentleman and the wording in section 13 from what is in the bill which is now before the house. If it is done by a bill rather than by resolution it is because the other method is more cumbersome. But, in fact, down the years the procedure has been to do it by bill as we have sought to do it this year.
The hon. member for Vancouver North asked a number of questions. He asked, first, why should the government appoint a private auditor? The answer will be found in section 13 of the Canadian National-Canadian Pacific Act which was passed in 1933 and amended in 1936. Section 13 (1) reads as follows:
A continuous audit of the accounts of national railways shall be made by independent auditors appointed annually by a joint resolution of the Senate and the House of Commons, and annually reporting to parliament in respect of their audit. Their annual report shall call attention to any
matters which in their opinion require consideration or remedial action. They shall be paid by the national company such amounts as the governor in council shall from time to time approve.
Therefore, in answer to his first question, why should the government appoint a private auditor? I say that ever since this act has been in force it has been the practice to put into effect the intention of this act, namely, that there should be appointed an independent firm of auditors. By "independent" I mean not only independent of the Canadian National Railways but, I think, independent of the auditor general. If that had not been the intention I think the act would have clearly stated that the auditor general should be appointed.
The hon. member asked two or three other questions. He said that the auditor general could do the work. I agree with him in that respect. I think the auditor general could do the work and could do a good job, but I do not agree that he could do a much better job; and I certainly cannot agree with the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson) who states that it would be a great saving of money to the taxpayers of Canada if the auditor general were appointed. I think I can disprove that point as I go along.
The Canadian National-Canadian Pacific Act clearly states that this shall be a continuing audit, which means that the auditors must be in office and in operation all the time. Continuity of auditors is not only advantageous to the national railways, but also necessary because of the nature of the business of the Canadian National Railways. Frequent changes of auditors in the Canadian National Railways would, I believe, be objectionable. Take, for instance, the position of the railways. They have over one hundred thousand employees. It is extremely big business, the railway comprising a large number of subsidiary companies, and there is a considerable diversity of operations. A considerable amount of time is spent over an extended period in auditing the accounts. There are no less than fifty people who are assigned to work on the auditing of the books of the Canadian National Railways, not in permanency it is true, but temporarily, while there are from five to ten men who are assigned to do that work permanently.
Does anyone in this house think for a moment that if the auditor general were to be assigned to do this work he could do it without having the same number of men? Unquestionably he could do it, but he would have to set up a staff of experts such as the firm of George A. Touche and Company employ, and if the auditor general were to set up this staff it

C.N.R.-Appointment of Auditors
would cost the country every bit as much money, and somewhat more, as I shall prove.
Because of the operations of the Canadian National in the United States, it is necessary to have accounting firms that have units in Duluth, Detroit and St. Albans, and the firms that do the auditing work for the Canadian National must have United States branches, or at least connections in the United States. George A. Touche and Company and some other auditing companies in the dominion have auditing units in the United States cities I have mentioned. The auditor general of Canada has not. It is true that the auditor general could employ auditors who would be contacts in those United States cities, but I submit that he would have to pay them far more money than the company which does the work for the Canadian National Railways.
There are not many auditing firms in Canada who, apart from having the necessary experience to do railway work, also have these accounting units in the United States. Then there is the great advantage in continuing one firm of auditors. I presume the house itself might be tempted to raise some objection to appointing the same firm, and I confess that I did not like the idea when I came to the department and saw this. But when I realized what a tumult and chaos would follow if the auditor were changed each year, I came to the conclusion that it was good business for the railways to keep in operation the same firm of auditors.
I said a moment ago that Touche and Company assign about fifty individuals to do the work, some of them only intermittently; but there are at least ten men in the city of Toronto who are assigned to do the work permanently, and four or five in the city of Montreal. If the auditor general were given this assignment he would have to work up a staff, a group of experts to do railway work. In other words, he would have to add to his staff the same number of men; no, I say a far greater number of men than that already employed by this firm of auditors.
There is another point I should like to make. The present firm of auditors also do the work of T.C.A., and under the Trans-Canada Air Lines Act the minister has discretion to appoint auditors. The minister under that act, as far as I can remember, has always appointed the same firm of auditors as the Canadian National. By doing that, he has saved the country money, because the one firm is able to do the work of the two corporations and thereby to do it far more cheaply.
It has been suggested that the auditor general is an excellent person; that he has qualifi-
|Mr. Chevrier.]
cations to do work of this kind, and with that I certainly would not disagree. On the contrary, I am entirely in agreement with my hon. friend when he says that Watson Sellar is a fine type of individual and one who is doing an excellent job as auditor general. With everything that the hon. member has said in that regard I am in full agreement. But where I differ with my hon. friend is on the statement that it would save the taxpayers of the country a substantial sum of money if we were to appoint the auditor general of Canada to do the auditing of the Canadian National Railways. I am informed that it would take the auditor general from two to three years to develop a staff to do this work properly. It is a fact that any new auditor-who might be put in the position of auditing the books of the Canadian National Railways should move in early in the year and be able to start from the beginning. The present auditors, George A. Touche and Company, as stated before, are doing continuous work and therefore have already started to audit the books for the year 1947. They are already in operation. That is by virtue of a practice which has existed over the years.
So that I must say to the house and to my hon. friend-and I agree with those who say that he has made an excellent presentation of his case-that the government cannot appoint a private auditor, because it is bound by section 13 of the Canadian National-Canadian Pacific Railway Act. I agree with the hon. member that the auditor general could do the job, but that the auditor general could do a much better job I have grave doubts; and certainly when the auditor general should find himself in the position of doing the job it would cost the taxpayers as much as, if not far more than, it costs the country at the moment through the appointment of this firm of auditors.
For that reason I must tell my hon. friend, if it will be of any assistance to him, that for the year 1948 I would be willing to inquire from the officers of my department, and at the same time consult the directors of the Canadian National Railways to ascertain whether it would not be possible to have the auditor general audit the accounts, but I am sure that if I were to discuss it with them they would place before me the reasons which I have now put before the house For these reasons I ask the house to approve the bill.

speechtext:
In rising to speak to the amendment, I am conscious that this gives me the most unusual chance for a private member to rebut the argument of a minister, but there are two or

C.N.R.-Appointment of Auditors
three points about the answer that has been given which strike me immediately. To begin with, the minister's first point was that I had asked for private auditors by resolution. Hon. members will realize that certainly that is not what I asked for. I asked for audit by the auditor general. I did not ask why private auditors did it, because I knew that was provided under the Canadian National Act, but I asked why the auditor general did not do it.
Because it has been done since 1933 by a private auditor is not a sufficient reason. The reason why I traced the development of the auditor general's position was to show that if perhaps he could not have done the job in 1933, he certainly was in a position to do it now.
The minister's comments about a resolution of parliament being the same as an act of parliament I find difficult to understand, and I can tell him I am in good company because the leader of the opposition in 1934, the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), advocated appointment by resolution of parliament and not by act of parliament submitted by the government. In 1936, the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, then leader of the opposition, advocated exactly the same thing. So that I am at least in good company, no matter what side of the house you judge my company from.
The second point was that the appointment of different auditors would result in an unhappy situation and that there would be no continuity of auditors. That was one of the points I was trying to make most strongly, because just as long as we have the Tory party appointing the firm of Clarkson and Company, the Liberal party appointing the firm of Touche and Company, and the C.C.F. government in some year far hence appointing some Saskatchewan firm, we shall not have continuity. We shall, however, have it if the auditor general is for all time appointed auditor for the companies.
The next point was one which fascinated me. It was to the effect that it would cost the government more to do that audit through the auditor general's department than through the firm of Touche and Company. Am I to understand that the firm of Touche and Company do that, at no profit? Or more than that, am I to understand that they do it at a loss because of their public spirit?

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OP GEORGE A. TOUCHE AND COMPANY AS AUDITORS
speechtext: They are more efficient.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OP GEORGE A. TOUCHE AND COMPANY AS AUDITORS
speechtext:
No one has denied that the auditor general is efficient. And no one can deny that the auditor general does not pay the salaries that George A. Touche and Company pay. The point about
George A. Touche and Company and their record is the very fact that they, according to the minister of railways in 1934, were the very ones who stirred up the agitation against the Clarkson firm so that they might have this apparently unprofitable audit.
The next point was with regard to staff. If there ever was a time when the auditor general's department had a qualified staff, it is now. They have the staff which did this enormous war work, although it is now being cut down. But they have a qualified staff at this time that they never had before. A point which I found out on inquiry was that, in the firm of Touche and Company, the great bulk of this work is done by juniors, either accountants in training or accountants just qualified. The thing in the minister's speech which shocked me a little was to find that in this day and age, under a government led by the grandson of William Lyon Mackenzie, there should still be one place in the expenditure of public moneys in which the appointment of an auditor was left to the minister's discretion, because in this report I quoted from a little earlier there is case after case in which William Lyon Mackenzie comments in the most scathing terms about the minister's audit and certifying to parliament, that this audit is proper, because in those days ministers of the crown either did the audit themselves in the department or appointed an auditor to do it.
The next point was that it would take two or three years for the auditor general's staff to get on to the job of auditing railway accounts. Again let us look at the record. In 1935. without notice, Doctor Manion changed the firm of George A. Touche and Company to the firm of Clarkson with the long name, and nobody on the Liberal or Conservative side in 1936 contended that this firm as Clarkson, without two or three years' experience in railway auditing, did not do just as good a job as George A. Touche. There was just the old joker, that from our point of view, probably the firm of George A. Touche was more satisfactory, just as Doctor Manion had said that the Clarkson firm was more satisfactory to his government than the firm of George A. Touche.
I did not ask for a change of private auditors. My point was simply that this audit of public funds should be done by the auditor general; and most certainly this parliament should see that no minister is left with the right to appoint an auditor for Trans-Canada Air Lines in this day and age, as apparently the Minister of Reconstruction is. Definitely that auditor should be at least appointed by

parliament, preferably by a resolution of parliament, and, best of all, should be the auditor general. For these reasons I see very little cause to change the stand which I took when I delivered my main address on this act.	[DOT]
